title: What the Parser Hears
dek: A configuration file has two readers: the person who writes it and the program that loads it. JSON, YAML and TOML each have places where the two hear different things. This is a field guide to all three as they stand in October 2026 — where each came from, what each can say, the pitfalls that still bite, measured by sending 71 cases through 34 parser configurations on this machine — and a rule for choosing among them.
byline: 9 October 2026 · Synthesised from the specifications, changelogs, issue trackers and maintainers' own words; 71 cases measured across 34 parser configurations in four languages on this machine; the XO examples are read from its tree
description: A field guide to JSON, YAML and TOML as configuration formats: their specs, their pitfalls, what 34 real parsers actually hear for the same bytes, and a practice for choosing and guarding a config format.
og_description: JSON, YAML and TOML for configuration, October 2026: where each came from, what each can express, the Norway problem and its cousins, TOML's table-scope trap and the 1.0/1.1 split, YAML's loader CVEs, round-trips that rewrite your data — measured across 34 parser configurations — and a practice that holds.
twitter_description: A config file has two readers. 71 cases, 34 parsers: where JSON, YAML and TOML make them hear different things, and how to choose.
badges_callout:
How to read the badges

from the spec marks a fact taken from a format's own specification: RFC 8259, ECMA-404, YAML 1.1 or 1.2.2, TOML 1.0.0 or 1.1.0. from the docs marks a fact from a project's documentation, changelog, issue tracker, CVE record, or a maintainer's own words. from the tree marks something read from the XO source trees on this machine, quoted with its path and line numbers. measured here marks a result produced on this machine, mostly by _compute.py beside this page: 71 cases sent through 34 parser configurations in Python 3.14 (and 3.15.0rc1 for one tomllib column), Node 24, Rust 1.97 and Go 1.27, plus jq, on one shared 2-CPU Linux machine. Some come from separate research probes on the same machine (spec word counts, git merges, Cargo publishing, the quoting and writer probes, the XO tree runs); the sentence or caption says so where they appear. What a parser heard is exact and repeatable; parse times are not, so they are given as tiers. reconstruction marks a judgement or mechanism I have worked out rather than read.

sections.title: Two readers, one file
sections.brief: Thesis in short declaratives: a configuration file has two readers, the person who writes it and the program that loads it, and every pitfall in this guide is a place where they hear different things. Three kinds of disagreement: syntax the author did not expect to matter (a BOM, a tab, a trailing comma), typing the author did not intend (NO becomes false, 3.10 becomes 3.1, 0755 becomes 493), and structure the author did not see (a key after a [table] header lands inside it; an indented first line truncates a Helm values file). A fourth arrives when programs write config back (agents, cargo add, uv add): the writer can change what the next reader hears. Introduce the measurement: 71 cases x 34 parser configurations; what a parser heard is exact and repeatable. Headline numbers to tease (all from _numbers.json / measure.md): `mode: 0755` has three readings across YAML loaders; the same 66-69-line agent config is heard identically by 28 of 32 parsers and the 4 that differ all turn the country code NO into false; a key appended after a TOML table header is silently moved into that table by all 10 TOML parser configurations. Then 'The answer, up front' (h3), so a reader can stop here: (1) for human-edited configuration of a tool you control, TOML, written to the 1.0 subset unless you pin the parser, top-level keys first; (2) for configuration a program writes or that crosses language boundaries, strict JSON validated by JSON Schema; if people also edit it in an editor, JSONC read by one named parser that fails on errors; (3) YAML only where the ecosystem expects it (Kubernetes by convention, GitHub Actions, Compose, Ansible), and then: quote every scalar that is not obviously a string, lint (yamllint truthy rule), validate against a schema, load with a YAML 1.2 safe loader with alias limits; (4) for all three: a schema, a strict loader that rejects duplicate and unknown keys, a typed target, and a CI check. Mark the recommendation as reconstruction. Mention the companion post ../where-the-json-lives/ (JSON as stored data) — this one is JSON as written configuration.

Mark the four disagreement points: syntax, typing, structure, write-back (a program dumping it back). Edge conventions: thin blue data, thick black control, dashed purple state/effect. sections.title: Three formats, three intentions
sections.brief: Where each came from and what it was designed to do; the design intent explains the pitfalls. JSON: Crockford, a data-interchange subset of JavaScript; RFC 4627 (2006), RFC 7159 (2014, top-level scalars allowed), RFC 8259 / STD 90 (2017) and ECMA-404 2nd ed. (2017). Crockford's Google+ post 'Comments in JSON' (30 April 2012, Wayback capture; quote verbatim from json.md F45-F49, F169-F170): comments removed because people used them for parsing directives; 'pipe it through JSMin' — and npm's rc does exactly that (lib/utils.js:15 JSON.parse(stripJsonComments(content))). YAML: 2001, first called 'Yet Another Markup Language', the 26 May 2001 draft says 'optimized for configuration settings' (ecosystem.md F13-F19); backronym by 2002; 1.0 2004-01-29, 1.1 'Final Draft' 2005-01-18 (yaml.org also says 2004-12-30), 1.2.0 2009-07-21, 1.2.1 2009-10-01, 1.2.2 2021-10-01 with no normative changes; no 1.3 exists. TOML: Tom Preston-Werner's first draft 2013-02-23 (Pacific) 'Tom's Own Markup Language ... like INI, only better', which called the YAML spec 'like 600 pages long' and Alex Gaynor corrected to 80 pages ~1h40m later; 0.5.0 2018, 1.0.0 January 2021, 1.1.0 2025-12-18 (CHANGELOG and toml.io; the git tag/GitHub release are 2025-12-24 — cite 12-18). Quote TOML's own goals from toml.io verbatim. Spec sizes measured in yaml.md section E (use their exact word counts; say how counted). PEP 518's rationale table is in a later section, do not duplicate.
figures: fig-timeline · 2001-2026 timeline (SVG, wide) · three lanes (JSON blue, YAML purple, TOML green); version ticks with dates; annotate Crockford comment removal 2012, YAML 1.2 2009, TOML 1.0 2021, TOML 1.1 2025-12-18, Python tomllib 3.11 (2022), Go json/v2 2026; a small inset bar of spec sizes in words (exact numbers from yaml.md section E).

sections.title: What each format can say
sections.brief: The data model is the contract's vocabulary. Compare precisely (cite spec sections): null (JSON null; YAML ~/null/empty under both schemas; TOML has none — #30: Preston-Werner 2013 'TOML is intended for configuration... just leave it out', Pradyun Gedam 2023-10-07 'we're not revisiting this design choice'; mitsuhiko #975: absence cannot express 'unset' in layered config; quote verbatim from toml.md section D); booleans (JSON true/false; YAML 1.2 Core six spellings; YAML 1.1 type repository 22 spellings and that page is itself a 'Working Draft'; TOML lowercase only); integers (JSON agnostic per ECMA-404, RFC 8259 interoperability note on binary64; YAML; TOML 64-bit recommended, and 1.1 clarified any size allowed); floats (NaN/inf absent from JSON, present in YAML .inf/.nan and TOML inf/nan); dates (none in JSON; YAML 1.1 timestamp type, not in 1.2 Core; TOML four types: offset date-time, local date-time, local date, local time); strings (JSON one kind; YAML plain/single/double/block | > with chomping; TOML four kinds); comments (none / # / #); references (YAML anchors/aliases and merge keys; none elsewhere); tags/types (YAML tags; none); top level (any value in JSON since RFC 7159; YAML any node; TOML always a table); duplicate keys (JSON SHOULD be unique; YAML MUST be unique; TOML invalid); version declaration (YAML %YAML directive — PyYAML ignores %YAML 1.2 for typing; JSON none; TOML none); key order (none guaranteed). Point out the asymmetry: JSON is a grammar with almost no semantics; YAML is a serialization language with a type-resolution step; TOML is a grammar with a fixed small type system. That is why JSON's pitfalls are reader disagreements, YAML's are type guesses, TOML's are structural.
figures: fig-type-matrix · what each format can express (HTML table, wide) · rows: null, booleans, integer range, NaN/inf, date-time, string kinds, multi-line strings, comments, references, tags, top-level, duplicate keys, version declaration, key order; columns: JSON (RFC 8259), YAML 1.1, YAML 1.2.2 Core, TOML 1.0, TOML 1.1. Short cell text; tint cells hl-red where a feature is a known trap, hl-green where it closes one.

sections.title: JSON: a strict grammar, loose readers
sections.brief: JSON's grammar is small and its readers disagree anyway. Spec text first (json.md section 1; quote exactly with section numbers): RFC 8259 §4 names 'SHOULD be unique' and the unpredictable behaviour sentence; §6 numbers interoperability; §8.1 UTF-8 'closed ecosystem' scoping and BOM; §9 parsers MAY accept extensions vs ECMA-404 §2 conformance wording. Neither spec contains the word 'comment'. Dialects for config (json.md section 3): JSONC (VS Code settings, tsconfig — tsc 7.0.2 accepts comments and trailing commas silently; jsonc-parser reports errors but still returns a value, even for a missing comma), JSON5, HJSON; strict JSON where it is chosen on purpose (package.json, Claude Code settings: comments or trailing commas are a Settings Error — quote docs), Node's node.config.json rejects duplicates; Go 1.27 json/v2 (Aug 2026) and Ruby json 3.0 (2026-09-07) moved to strict-by-default; ESLint v10 (2026-02-06) removed .eslintrc.json. Measured (_numbers.json cases j_*; measure.md): duplicate keys — last wins in Python, JSON.parse, jq, jsonc-parser, json5; Go v2/serde struct/Ruby 3/node.config.json reject; Go v1 merges a duplicate object into a struct field and matches keys case-insensitively (json.md F91-F104; note which were measured by the json research probes vs the harness); 2^53+1 rounded by JS and Go untyped; a u64 id has three spellings for one double (12345678901234567168 printed as 12345678901234567000 by JS and 1.2345678901234567e+19 by Go); Python json.dumps writes NaN/Infinity by default, which JSON.parse, jsonc-parser, serde_json, Go reject and jq turns into null and 1.7976931348623157e+308; 1e400; BOM (Python str vs bytes asymmetry; PowerShell 5.1 writes UTF-16LE — json.md F124-F128); lone surrogate (Go v1 -> U+FFFD); key order three ways (JS integer-like keys first); depth limits from json5 at 60 and serde_json 128 up to JSON.parse at 100,000+. __proto__: JSON.parse makes it an own key, but deep-merge of config layers pollutes; rc uses deep-extend (CVE-2018-3750); jsonc-parser installs a __proto__ payload as the object's prototype (CVE-2022-46175 class) — measured. Diff/merge cost of no trailing commas (json.md F144-F147, measured with git 2.55). Include one short code excerpt of a probe (≤15 lines) with its path in _compute.py or the _cases file and line numbers.

sections.title: YAML: the type you did not write
sections.brief: YAML resolves every plain scalar to a type by matching regular expressions, and which expressions depends on the schema version the loader implements — not on the file. Quote the YAML 1.1 bool regexp from yaml.org/type/bool.html verbatim and the 1.2.2 Core schema tag resolution table (yaml.md sections B, C). The Norway problem: origin in StrictYAML docs (earliest found use 2018-11-03 commit; the source is a second-hand anecdote — say so); StrictYAML's page wrongly says it is 1.2 behaviour (yaml.md myths #1). Library landscape on 2026-10-08 (yaml.md section G; quote READMEs): PyYAML 6.0.3 (2025-09-25) still 1.1 but not y/n; ruamel 0.19.1 1.2 default but still resolves 0b, _ and dates; js-yaml 4 mostly 1.2 core + timestamp + merge; js-yaml 5.0.0 (2026-06-20) pure CORE_SCHEMA, merge off; eemeli yaml 2.9.1 1.2 with 1.1 option; go-yaml v3 'most of YAML 1.2' but 1.1 bools into typed bool fields; go-yaml archived 2025-04-01, continued as go.yaml.in/yaml v4 (Compose uses it); sigs.k8s.io/yaml (Kubernetes) on go-yaml v2 with full 1.1 bools incl. single letters; serde_yaml archived; serde-saphyr 1.3.0 (2026-09-16) reads NO/y/n/on/off as booleans by default (strict_booleans false). Measured scalar cases (y_norway, y_bools, y_octal, y_sexagesimal, y_versions, y_exponent, y_underscore, y_inf_nan, y_nulls, y_timestamps, y_zip): give the actual readings — mode 0755 three readings (493 / 755 / '0755'); ZIP codes four readings; 22:22 -> 1342 in PyYAML; 3.10 -> 3.1 in every typed loader under both 1.1 and 1.2 (setup-python issue #482 title 'Python version 3.10 is parsed as "3.1"'); 1e3 is the string '1e3' in PyYAML but 1000 in 1.2 loaders. Quoting is the only mitigation that works everywhere: all 16 loader rows return quoted text as a string (yaml.md). The %YAML 1.2 directive does not help (PyYAML ignores it). Close with the writer/reader asymmetry teaser: a 1.2 writer emits NO unquoted and a 1.1 reader hears false (detailed in the round-trip section).

sections.title: YAML: the structure you did not see
sections.brief: Indentation and document structure can change meaning without an error. Measured cases (measure.md digest + _numbers.json): helm#9793 reproduced in 2026 — a values.yaml whose first line is indented two spaces is silently truncated to its first mapping by yaml.v3 v3.0.1, sigs.k8s.io/yaml v1.6.0 (Helm 3.6's ReadValues path) and serde-saphyr 1.3.0; nine loaders error. Constructed mis-indented list (y_misindent_list). Multi-document input to single-document APIs: yaml.v3, sigs, goccy return the first document silently; nine error; kubernetes#103185 explained as reconstruction. '--- # comment' separator report (y_separator_comment). sigs.k8s.io/yaml renames map key y to "true" ({x:1, y:2} -> {x:1, "true":2}). The `on:` key: PyYAML loads it as True and yamllint's truthy rule flags it, but GitHub's public workflow parser reads it as the string 'on' and GitHub's docs use unquoted on: everywhere — so 'GitHub Actions breaks on on:' is a myth; the risk is your own tooling reading the workflow (yaml.md myth #8; tree.md found 3 XO files and 29 upstream with bare on:). The '!.git' entry from 'The YAML document from hell' (Ruud van Asseldonk, 2023-01-11) silently becomes '' in every go-yaml version, sigs and eemeli yaml (with a warning); PyYAML and js-yaml raise — measured, confirming the essay; quote the essay's thesis briefly. Values containing ': ' and ' #'; tab indentation (forbidden by spec — what loaders do); block scalars and chomping (| |- > >-, measured output); duplicate keys (spec MUST unique; PyYAML, go-yaml v2, non-strict sigs keep last silently); merge keys << are not YAML 1.2 (2005 working draft type only) and GitHub Actions does not support them (GitHub Changelog 2025-09-18 for anchors support — check ecosystem.md F146-F147). Kubernetes ConfigMap: an unquoted bool in data fails loudly on the API path but sigs.k8s.io/yaml.Unmarshal into map[string]string coerces it to "false" (yaml.md).

Exact keys from the y_misindent_helm9793 case.

sections.title: When loading means executing
sections.brief: YAML tags let a document name a constructor; that is the root of a decade of CVEs. Chain (yaml.md section I; quote NVD/GHSA descriptions verbatim): CVE-2017-18342 (PyYAML yaml.load unsafe by default); PyYAML 5.1 YAMLLoadWarning and FullLoader; FullLoader bypasses CVE-2019-20477, CVE-2020-1747, CVE-2020-14343; PyYAML 6.0 made Loader mandatory; SnakeYAML CVE-2022-1471 (NVD CVSS 9.8; CNA 8.3) fixed in 2.0 by blocking global tags; Ruby Psych 4 / Ruby 3.1 made load mean safe_load; js-yaml 4 removed !!js/function (measured y_js_function). Measured: y_python_tag harmless payload — what safe_load, full_load, unsafe_load, ruamel safe did. Denial of service is not covered by 'safe': CVE-2019-11253 (Kubernetes) 9^9 alias bomb, 'YAML or JSON' per NVD, fixed with decode limits and a 3 MB body cap; measured y_bomb9 (446 B): PyYAML C and pure, ruamel safe/rt, js-yaml 4/5 and goccy load it as shared references (graph of 435,848,053 leaves); eemeli yaml (maxAliasCount 100), yaml.v3 and sigs (alias-ratio heuristic), serde_yaml (repetition limit) and serde-saphyr (max_nodes 250,000) refuse it; y_bomb6: 335 B materialises into 4,334,696 B of JSON. PyYAML 6.0.3 safe_load is exponential on nested merge keys: a 673-byte document took seconds (state the measured range and the 'orders of magnitude' caveat from yaml.md F177 correction); fix merged to main 2026-06-17, not in any PyPI release as of 2026-10-08. js-yaml merge-key advisories (yaml.md F179, careful wording: 'quadratic' only where the advisory says so). JSON's analogue is prototype pollution in config merging (cross-reference the JSON section, do not repeat). TOML has no tags, aliases or constructors; its DoS surface is nesting depth (Rust toml 80, tomlkit 100, tomli 401; BurntSushi and @iarna accept 100,000).
figures: fig-cve-ledger · a decade of loader CVEs (HTML table, wide) · CVE, library, year, what the payload did, CVSS (state source), fixed in, and whether 'safe' mode covered it.

sections.title: TOML: obvious until the second table
sections.brief: TOML's grammar is small and its type system fixed, so its pitfalls are structural. TOML's stated goals are quoted in the lineages section — link to #lineages instead of quoting them again. The scope trap: keys after a [table] header belong to that table until the next header; a top-level key appended at the end of a file silently becomes server.debug. Measured: all 10 TOML parser configurations in the harness do it silently (t_scope_trap); toml.md's wider research probe found the same in 16 configurations — say which count is which; Cargo 1.97.1 and pytest 9.1.1 only warn on the unknown key (tree.md probes); Alacritty created a [general] section in 2024 (PR #8192) because 'root options must always be at the top of the file, since they're otherwise associated with the last table' (quote verbatim from toml.md); Zola's docs warn about the same rule; tree.md F79: appending workspace.exclude to makepad's Cargo.toml lands at profile.test.package.makepad-stitch.workspace.exclude. Table redefinition, [a.b] before [a] (valid), dotted key into a [table]-defined table (invalid), [table] over a dotted-key table, extending an inline table (invalid; inline tables are immutable), arrays of tables [[x]] vs [x]. Measured disagreements: BurntSushi v1.6.0 accepts two documents the spec calls invalid; @iarna/toml 2.2.5 (npm latest, TOML 0.5, 2020) accepts the spec's own '# [fruit.apple]  # INVALID' example. Integers: 64-bit; @iarna wraps 9223372036854775808 to -9223372036854775808n; the Python family returns the exact big int; Rust/Go/smol error; smol-toml refuses even i64::MAX and 2^53+1 by default (lossless rule). 0755 invalid vs 0o755. Floats inf/nan/-0.0. Mixed-type arrays allowed since 1.0. Four date-time types and what native type each parser returns (t_datetimes); smol-toml and @iarna turn 2020-02-30 into 2020-03-01 (toml.md). True is invalid. No null: 'x = ' is an error everywhere; writers disagree on null — tomli_w and tomlkit raise, smol-toml and @iarna drop null keys and @iarna turns [1, null] into [1], go-toml v2 writes []*int{&1, nil} as ports = [1, 0] (toml.md). CRLF inside multi-line strings: Python family normalises vs 7 keep. Deep nesting verbosity (Kubernetes-shaped data is painful in TOML; say why with a 6-line example). BOM splits parsers 8 to 8. tomlkit reads '1' + Arabic-Indic zero as 10 (toml.md) — verify in dossier before using.

sections.title: TOML 1.1 and the version nobody declares
sections.brief: TOML 1.1.0 (2025-12-18) is the first release in almost five years; quote the CHANGELOG lines verbatim (toml.md F22-F25): newlines and trailing commas in inline tables (#904), \xHH (#796), \e (#790), optional seconds in times (#894), plus clarifications ('Parsers must not modify keys or values' based on comments; any int/float size allowed, int64/binary64 recommended). History: multi-line inline tables merged 2022-07 but unreleased until 2025-12; Unicode bare keys merged 2022 (#891) and backed out 2025 (#979). A TOML file cannot declare its version, so a 1.0 parser reports 1.1 syntax as a generic syntax error. Measured (t_inline_multiline, t_escape_e, t_escape_x, t_time_no_seconds): Python 3.14.4 tomllib and @iarna reject all four; tomllib in 3.15.0rc1, tomli 2.5.0 and every Rust, Go and smol parser accept. Python: tomllib reads 1.0.0 in 3.11-3.14 and 1.1.0 from 3.15 (gh-142956); PEP 790 schedules 3.15.0 final for 2026-10-09 — CHECK python.org at writing time and state the status precisely with the time you checked. tomli added 1.1 in 2.4.0 (2026-01-11), tomlkit 0.15.0 (2026-05-10), BurntSushi v1.6.0 made 1.1 default (2025-12-18), go-toml v2.4.0 (2026-06-17), smol-toml v1.6.0 (2025-12-22), Rust toml 0.9.10 / toml_edit 0.24.0 on release day. Cargo reads TOML 1.1 manifests since 1.94 (2026-03-05) and says the published manifest 'remains compatible with older parsers' — but measured on Cargo 1.97.1, the normalized published Cargo.toml kept the seconds-less datetime built = 2026-10-08T14:15, which tomllib on 3.14 rejects (toml.md; quote and show). toml-test results (toml.md section E, suite at ff49d10): tomli 2.5.0 and 3.15rc1 tomllib 218/218 valid and 494/494 invalid in 1.1 mode; npm toml 5.0.0 218/486; smol-toml 218/480; tomlkit 217/486; BurntSushi 216/478; 3.14 tomllib perfect in 1.0 mode (208/208, 501/501). application/toml registered with IANA 2024-10-21 with no RFC; 'TOML as an RFC?' (#870) still open. Practical rule: write the 1.0 subset unless you pin the parser; or check with tomllib on the oldest Python you support. Put the per-parser 1.1 adoption dates in the fig-toml-11 table as a 'learned 1.1' column instead of a separate timeline.

sections.title: One configuration, three ways
sections.brief: Put the formats side by side on a realistic file: _cases/cross/agent.{json,yaml,toml} — an agent-service config (model, timeouts, retry, routing.allowed_countries, a multi-line system prompt, MCP servers with env maps, a datetime). Show excerpts side by side (the same ~20 lines in each format; escape HTML). Sizes: JSON 1,707 B / 69 lines, YAML 1,525 B / 66, TOML 1,560 B / 67 (_numbers.json cross_format.files). 28 of 32 parsers hear the same data as agent.json; the 4 that differ (PyYAML safe and CSafeLoader, sigs.k8s.io/yaml, serde-saphyr) all read allowed_countries[4] as false — the Norway problem in a real-looking file. Parse time: give tiers, not precise numbers, and state the method (median of 501 parses after 50 warm-ups) and the caveat that the CPU was shared with another tenant so medians moved up to 2.7x between runs; tiers: fastest JSON parsers ~10-50 µs, TOML parsers ~20 µs to a few ms (tomlkit slowest), YAML ~100 µs to ~10 ms (ruamel rt slowest; PyYAML pure ~10x slower than CSafeLoader) — derive exact tier bounds from _numbers.json cross_format.timing and say they are order-of-magnitude. Conclusion: for config, parse time almost never matters; what matters is what is heard. Then the MCP example: the same thing — a list of MCP servers — has three shapes across agent tools: mcpServers in claude_desktop_config.json and .mcp.json, servers in VS Code .vscode/mcp.json, [mcp_servers.<id>] tables in Codex config.toml (ecosystem.md F121, F125, F132-F133). Nesting cost: TOML repeats the full path in headers ([mcp_servers.github.env]); JSON/YAML nest.

sections.title: When the program writes back
sections.brief: Config is no longer only read: cargo add, uv add, poetry add, Codex, Wrangler and editors write it, and agents now edit it too. PEP 680 states the round-trip argument: tomllib is read-only because editing human TOML needs a style-preserving parser, and tomlkit was rejected for the stdlib (quote ecosystem.md F44-F45). Who writes how (ecosystem.md section G, tree.md): Codex writes config.toml with toml_edit; Wrangler patches JSONC with jsonc-parser but refuses to edit a wrangler.toml containing any '#' because smol-toml drops comments — a substring test, so color = "#fff" also blocks it (F59-F61); Gemini CLI reads with strip-json-comments (accepts comments, rejects trailing commas) and writes with comment-json; VS Code edits text with setProperty; Claude Code keeps settings.json strict JSON. cargo add and uv add keep comments but insert keys in sorted order, and cargo placed a new dependency above a comment that belonged to serde (F111-F112). Measured round trip (_numbers.json roundtrip; measure.md F94-F104): load, edit one value, dump on the 66-69-line agent config — tomlkit and jsonc-parser modify are byte-identical except the edit; toml_edit's idiomatic value() assignment drops the edited line's comment (2 diff lines); ruamel rt 38-line diff by default, 4 with indentation configured; PyYAML safe_dump sorts keys, drops all six comments and writes false for NO, so no later reader can recover the intent; serde_json, Go and yaml.v3 Marshal sort keys; tomli_w drops comments, rewrites 0o5432 as 2842 and moves [[jobs]] to an inline array at the top; JS round-trips rewrite timeout = 1.0 as timeout = 1. Cross-version emitters: eemeli yaml 2.9.1, ruamel and serde_yaml write NO, yes, on and 22:22 unquoted (correct for 1.2), and PyYAML reads them back as false, true, 1342; PyYAML writes the string 1e3 unquoted and 1.2 readers hear 1000; goccy writes .inf and 1e3 unquoted. Only yaml.v3, sigs, serde-saphyr and js-yaml 5 survive all three readers. Rule: a tool that writes human config must use a format-preserving editor, or refuse, or own the file outright. Fold the cross-version emitter results (NO/yes/22:22/1e3 written by one library and read by another) into the fig-roundtrip table or a compact prose table; no separate figure.

sections.title: What our own tree says
sections.brief: Ground everything in the XO trees on this machine (tree.md; cite path:line exactly as the dossier gives, re-open the file to confirm lines before quoting). Counts: 304 config-shaped files, 230 in XO-owned trees; 199 of the 230 are JSON but only 55 are config a person writes (66 .xo watcher state, 60 data/artifacts, 14 schemas, 4 lockfiles); XO trees have 10 YAML files and exactly 1 TOML file (fly-lab/pyproject.toml); upstream clones lean the other way (36 YAML, 8 TOML of 74). The biggest finding: xo-space's agent manifests point at four config formats (Claude JSON, Codex TOML, Hermes YAML, OpenClaw JSON5); the Settings->Config route (routers/cowork_agent/config.py:256-261) picks a parser by suffix; a valid Codex config.toml returns HTTP 500 and a JSON5 openclaw.json returns 500; adapters/openclaw/store.py:27-35 turns any parse failure into {} and create_agent (agents.py:156-183) then wrote that back — in a scratch HOME it replaced the whole openclaw.json with only agents.list. Describe precisely and neutrally, as a measured finding in a scratch environment, not as an incident. .env has no single grammar: 7 hand-written parsers plus python-dotenv plus a bash loop; on the same 12-line file five disagree about inline comments, quotes, export and spaces; a secret saved through the Settings UI as 'p@ss #1' is 'p@ss' after restart (xo_projects_sync/config.py:94-97 writes values unquoted); duplicated keys edited first-row but read last-row. Precedence: the server.py:29-31 comment says shell exports outrank files but runtime.env and secrets.env load with override=True (measured); boolean env vars use two vocabularies (on enables QUIRQ_WATCHER_ENABLED but not UVICORN_RELOAD). YAML typing reaches secret masking: _mask_sensitive (helpers.py:205-223) only masks strings, so password: 123456 came back unmasked as an int in a scratch Hermes config. fly-lab: YAML + JSON twins load identically (5 pairs), CLI overrides through ast.literal_eval give a third reading (010 stays a string, null is 'null', 3.10 -> 3.1). The only Norway-style pitfall in XO YAML is the bare on: key (3 files). quirq: the outcome spec (B, weighted checks, tau) is not represented in any config yet; the same spec written in JSON, TOML and YAML parses to equal dicts; with weights 0.7/0.1/0.2 and tau = 0.8, V comes out 0.7999999999999999 and done = False in Python and Node — a decimal-to-binary edge, not a format difference (quote section-2-spec.md lines for the fields). Propose (reconstruction) the quirq outcome spec as a TOML file (≤20 lines) with weights as integers or a rational convention, and show it. Do NOT mention the personal ~/.claude contents beyond what tree.md states about structure; never print secret values or key names that look sensitive.

sections.title: A practice that holds
sections.brief: Turn the guide into rules, each tied to a measured or sourced failure above. Universal: (1) name the parser and its version — the format is not the contract, the parser is; (2) validate against a schema in CI and in the editor — SchemaStore's catalog (snapshot 2026-10-08) has 1,513 schemas, 762 matching YAML files, 624 JSON-family, 128 TOML; JSON Schema 2020-12 is still the current dialect (an Internet-Draft that expired Dec 2022); VS Code says a $schema key in the file is VS Code-specific; taplo / Tombi for TOML, yaml-language-server, check-jsonschema; (3) load into a typed target and reject unknown keys (serde deny_unknown_fields, Go DisallowUnknownFields / json/v2, pydantic extra=forbid) — this catches the TOML scope trap and YAML truncation; (4) reject duplicate keys; (5) never write human config with a non-preserving writer; (6) keep secrets out of config files that agents read and write. JSON rules: strict where machines write; JSONC only with one named parser that fails on errors; never let Python write NaN (allow_nan=False); ids as strings beyond 2^53; UTF-8 without BOM. YAML rules: quote everything that is not obviously a string (versions, codes, modes, times, anything starting with 0 or !); YAML 1.2 safe loader with alias limits; yamllint with truthy and key-duplicates; actionlint for workflows; never yaml.load; avoid merge keys; one document per file unless the API is multi-document. TOML rules: top-level keys first (or a [general] table as Alacritty did); write the 1.0 subset unless you pin a 1.1 parser; no null — decide on absence vs sentinel and document it; integers within int64 and, if JS reads them, within 2^53; dates with offsets. Then 'When none of the three fits' (h3): one line each, from ecosystem.md section D, with verified dates/versions: JSON5, HCL (Terraform; HCL v2 tagged 2019-10-02), CUE, Dhall, Jsonnet, Nickel, Pkl (Apple, open-sourced Feb 2024), KDL, StrictYAML, NestedText (3.8, 2025-12-26), Starlark; and the ESLint path: config as code (eslint.config.js). Close with the decision rule paragraph (reconstruction) that mirrors the answer up front.
